strengths: The paper addresses a practical and important problem: efficient visual grounding with small VLMs, showing consistent gains across multiple model families (InternVL and Qwen) and model sizes.

The proposed EGM pipeline is clear and reproducible in broad outline: GPT-4-generated reasoning traces for SFT, followed by GRPO-style RL with learnability-based hard sample selection and a combined IoU/success reward.
The empirical results are strong on RefCOCO benchmarks: EGM-Qwen3-VL-8B reaches 91.4 average accuracy, outperforming Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B while being significantly cheaper in total GPU-time.
The paper introduces and evaluates an amodal grounding setting for VLMs, generating text prompts from COCO-Amodal/TAO-Amodal and showing consistent improvements across models.
Qualitative examples illustrate how reasoning helps resolve ‘COMPLEX_PROMPT’ failures, and the failure-mode analysis provides useful motivation, even if not fully rigorous.
weaknesses: The central claim of 'scaling test-time inference' is not adequately supported: there is no scaling analysis showing accuracy as a function of generated tokens, compute, or sampling budget. The method mainly trains a reasoning model; it does not demonstrate test-time scaling curves or compare with self-consistency/search baselines.

Missing ablation of the reasoning component: the paper does not isolate gains from the GPT-4 reasoning traces versus additional SFT data, RL, or hard-sample selection. A 'SFT without reasoning' baseline is needed to justify the claimed source of improvement.

The efficiency claim is potentially misleading because 'GPU latency' is defined as latency multiplied by number of GPUs, which is a total-compute measure, not end-to-end wall-clock latency. The abstract/claims of 5.9x faster inference may overstate deployment speed.

The failure-mode analysis relies on GPT-4 to categorize failures, with no human validation, no inter-annotator agreement, and no analysis of Qwen failure distributions; the conclusion that COMPLEX_PROMPT is the dominant cause may not generalize across model families.

The new amodal grounding benchmark is generated and verified entirely by GPT-4, with about 50% filtering, but lacks human validation, detailed annotation protocol, and analysis of prompt quality. Large InternVL models scoring far below 8B (e.g., 38B: 36.0, 78B: 51.0) further raises concerns about benchmark and prompting consistency.

Novelty is limited relative to existing work: the method combines off-the-shelf SFT, GRPO/RL, and GPT-4 distillation without substantial technical innovation. The framing as a new scaling paradigm is stronger than the algorithmic contribution.
Reproducibility is weakened by code/data/website being 'coming soon'; the training data and generated reasoning traces are not released, and key data curation details depend on proprietary models.

The presented analysis for why small VLMs lag is suggestive but not conclusive; it is not tested whether visual encoder differences or other training data differences also contribute, and it does not rigorously separate language understanding from visual representation quality.

strengths: The problem is well motivated and practically relevant: making small grounding VLMs competitive with much larger ones at lower deployment cost is a worthwhile and timely goal.

The empirical results are broad and consistent: EGM is applied to six checkpoints across two families (InternVL-3 and Qwen3-VL) and improves vanilla and amodal grounding in almost all cases, which is a non-trivial amount of evidence for the general applicability of the recipe.

The proposed amodal grounding setting (predict the full extent of an occluded referred object) is a reasonable and underexplored task for VLM-based referring, and the curation pipeline with a GPT-4 verification filter (App. B, Fig. 7-9) is a sensible first-pass construction.
The paper documents implementation details (SFT/RL hyperparameters, rollout settings, prompt templates, dataset sizes), which makes re-implementation of the two-stage SFT+GRPO recipe plausible.
Qualitative examples (Fig. 10-11) are informative and illustrate the intended behavior (key-feature-focused reasoning) versus the verbose reasoning of the 235B thinking model.
weaknesses: The central framing is not supported by the experiments. The title and abstract advertise "scaling test-time inference" / "#generated tokens" as the mechanism, but the gains come from supervised fine-tuning on GPT-4-generated reasoning traces plus GRPO reinforcement learning, i.e. a training-time recipe. No controlled test-time scaling (budget forcing, self-consistency, best-of-N, extra sampling at inference) is performed, and EGM is never compared against simply spending more inference compute on the untrained model; hence the headline claim about test-time scaling is not demonstrated.

The technical method has little novelty relative to the existing literature: answer-conditioned GPT-4 reasoning distillation plus GRPO is exactly the R1-style recipe (Guo et al. [15], Shao et al. [33], and the learnability-based data selection of Evans et al. [14]) transplanted to grounding. Prior reasoning/RL-for-grounding work (e.g. VLM-R1, Visual-RFT, Vision-R1, Seg-Zero and related GRPO-for-perception papers) is neither cited nor used as a baseline, so the paper's incremental position is unclear.

The diagnostic that motivates the paper (Sec. 3, Table 1, Fig. 2) is not adequately validated. Failure categories ("COMPLEX_PROMPT" 62.8%) are produced by asking GPT-4 to label failures, with no human verification, no agreement statistics, no confidence calibration, and an unstated subset size; the claim that small VLMs fail because of text understanding rather than visual handling is inferred from "visual encoders are similar" rather than tested with a controlled experiment (e.g., giving the small model a disambiguated description, or holding visual ability fixed).

Table 1 actively contradicts the paper's scaling narrative and is left uncommented: Gemini-2.5-Pro (22.1%) and Gemini-2.5-Flash (20.9%) are worse on the same COMPLEX_PROMPT failures than InternVL-3-32B (29.9%) and InternVL-3-78B (42.6%). If a frontier model underperforms a 32B open model by 20 points on this subset, the subset is more plausibly dominated by dataset/prompt-format artifacts than by "size"; the authors never discuss this, even though it undermines the stated rationale.

The same anomaly affects Table 3, raising questions about the evaluation protocol: GPT-5 averages 42.6 and Gemini-2.5-Pro 63.8 RefCOCO/+/g accuracy while Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct reaches 84.2. A single prompt template derived from the InternVL/Qwen formats (Fig. 5) applied to API models is very likely to break their output parsing, and in Table 3 the InternVL baseline numbers are taken from official reports (marked *) while all EGM numbers are self-measured, mixing measurement sources within the same comparison. The reported conclusion of EGM superiority, especially margins of ~1 point, is therefore not trustworthy as-is.

There are no ablations whatsoever. SFT-only vs. RL-only vs. SFT+RL, reasoning-trace quality/faithfulness, the learnability-based data selection (vs. random/uniform selection), the reward weighting alpha, and the effect of reasoning length are all untested, so no component of the method can be attributed with the observed gains.

The amodal benchmark and metric do not establish that the task is non-trivially solved. The evaluation set is constructed by the same proprietary VLM pipeline used to build the training data (text prompts generated and self-verified by GPT-4, ~50% filtered), the only metric is a 0.5-IoU success rate on amodal boxes, and there is no baseline showing that simply predicting the visible (modal) box cannot already pass this criterion, nor any comparison to classical amodal detection on COCO-Amodal/TAO-Amodal. The "we are the first to study amodal grounding in VLMs" claim is asserted rather than substantiated against prior amodal/VLM work.

The headline quantitative claim is fragile: "EGM-Qwen3-VL-8B achieves 91.4 IoU vs. Qwen3-VL-235B's 90.5" rests on a 0.9-point difference on a thresholded accuracy metric with no error bars, no multiple seeds, and no significance testing, and the abstract mislabels this accuracy (fraction of samples with IoU>0.5) as "IoU". A ~1-point margin over a model 30x larger should not be presented as outperforming it without variance estimates.

The efficiency argument is incompletely evidenced. Only EGM-vs-235B latency is reported; there is no comparison of EGM latency/token count against the vanilla small model it replaces, which is the relevant cost of the added reasoning, nor any accounting for the substantial one-off cost of generating 575K GPT-4 reasoning traces and running GRPO. The "GPU latency in practice = latency x number of GPUs" metric is unconventional and favors multi-GPU baselines without justification.

Distillation data has a potential answer-leakage problem: reasoning traces are generated by a teacher that is shown the ground-truth box (Fig. 6, "The image shows a green bounding box indicating the Ground Truth target object"), so the traces are rationalizations of a known answer rather than reasoning toward it. The paper does not analyze whether the student learns generalizable localization reasoning or dataset-specific cues, and the marginal gains for some models (e.g. InternVL-3-8B, +1.1 avg) are consistent with the latter.

Reproducibility is limited: the promised code/website are placeholders ("coming soon" on the first page), and core steps (reasoning generation, amodal prompt generation, failure categorization) depend on a proprietary VLM, so no part of the pipeline as described can be fully reproduced from the submission.

The manuscript is visibly unfinished: leftover placeholder links, duplicated/empty table cells and typos in tabular material ("INTernVL", "GGemini"), incomplete reference entries (e.g. [2] "Qwen3-vl, 2025" with no venue/link), and over-claimed statements in the introduction and conclusion.

strengths: Identifies a practically important failure mode ('COMPLEX_PROMPT') for small VLMs on visual grounding and provides reasonable empirical motivation.

Introduces EGM, an SFT+RL reasoning pipeline that consistently improves multiple small VLM families and sizes on RefCOCO, with strong efficiency gains (e.g., 8B model beats 235B while being 5.9x faster).
Extends the study to a new amodal grounding setting and curates corresponding training/evaluation data, showing consistent improvements over base models.
Evaluation covers several model families, sizes, benchmarks, and qualitative examples, supporting generality of the approach.
The paper is generally clear and well organized.
weaknesses: The 'test-time scaling' framing is somewhat misleading: the method primarily trains a reasoning model rather than dynamically scaling inference-time computation (e.g., by varying token budgets, voting, or search). No test-time scaling curve is provided.

Methodological novelty is limited: using GPT-4-generated chain-of-thought plus GRPO for grounding is an application of existing techniques. There is no ablation isolating SFT vs. RL, reasoning traces vs. direct fine-tuning, or reward components.

Data and benchmark curation rely heavily on proprietary GPT-4 for generating reasoning traces and amodal prompts/verification, with no human validation or detailed quality analysis. The new amodal benchmark may inherit GPT-4 biases and has potential circularity since both training and evaluation data are generated by the same proprietary model.

Reproducibility is incomplete: code and data are 'coming soon'; key details such as data splits, prompt templates, filtering criteria, and generated data statistics are only partially specified, and there are citation/typo issues (e.g., RefCOCO data reference).

The failure analysis uses GPT-4 to categorize selected failures without human verification, so the 62.8% COMPLEX_PROMPT statistic and the broad conclusion that language understanding is the main gap are suggestive but not rigorously established.

The efficiency comparison lacks a detailed breakdown of latency and token counts for base small models versus EGM reasoning models, making it hard to assess the true overhead and practicality of longer reasoning.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: efficient visual grounding VLMs for deployment, with a clear SFT+RL approach and latency comparison.

Empirical results are broad across two VLM families and multiple model sizes, showing consistent improvement on RefCOCO/RefCOCO+/RefCOCOg, with EGM-Qwen3-VL-8B surpassing much larger models on accuracy and latency.
Extends the method to amodal grounding, curating a new benchmark/training setup and demonstrating improvements on a task with less existing VLM grounding work.
Provides implementation details, hyperparameters, prompts, qualitative examples, and ablations for SFT/RL and the reasoning component.
weaknesses: The central diagnosis that small VLMs fail mainly because of 'COMPLEX-PROMPT'/language understanding is not rigorously established. The failure categorization is subjective, relies on proprietary models that disagree substantially, analyzes only InternVL-3-8B, and lacks controlled experiments isolating visual encoder vs. LLM capacity.

Data curation depends on an unspecified proprietary VLM, and vanilla reasoning traces are generated conditioned on ground-truth boxes, potentially producing post-hoc rationalizations rather than causal grounding reasoning. This harms reproducibility, attribution, and confidence in the distilled supervision.

The reasoning ablation is inconsistent: in Table 10, the '+EGM w/o R' variant sometimes underperforms the base model or yields only small gains, so the claim that reasoning consistently and significantly improves performance is overstated. Gains may come from extra SFT/RL data rather than reasoning.

Comparisons with proprietary models are not convincing: they are evaluated with limited prompt tuning and very low scores (e.g., GPT-5 40.1), while the paper simultaneously claims it is hard to distill from inferior models, creating a tension with its use of proprietary VLMs for data generation.

Efficiency claims are not fully supported: latency is measured only on L20 GPUs, edge-deployment claims are not tested, and there is no analysis of the token-quality/token-quantity tradeoff or comparison to other efficient inference/distillation/test-time scaling methods.

The new amodal grounding benchmark is generated using the same proprietary pipeline used for training data, with no human verification and about 50% filtering; this risks distributional bias and makes the evaluation less trustworthy.

There are clarity and reproducibility issues: missing code/model links, unspecified commercial VLM versions, citation errors, and confusing table values (e.g., improvements displayed as '+0.07' while text claims '+6.0').
No limitations or societal-impact discussion is provided, and there is no failure analysis of the proposed EGM models beyond qualitative examples.

strengths: Targets an important practical problem: efficient visual grounding for deployment, with a clear motivation around small vs. large VLMs.

Reports consistent empirical gains across multiple model families and sizes (Qwen3-VL and InternVL) on RefCOCO/+/g, with some improvements being substantial (e.g., +6.0 average accuracy for Qwen3-VL-2B).
Extends the evaluation to amodal grounding, an underexplored setting, and shows improvements over the base VLMs.
Provides an efficiency comparison suggesting that an 8B reasoning model can match or exceed a much larger 235B model while being significantly faster at inference.
Implementation details, hyperparameters, and prompt templates are partially documented in the appendix, which aids some reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core hypothesis that small VLMs fall behind mainly due to language understanding rather than visual encoding is not rigorously supported. The failure analysis relies on proprietary VLM labels that disagree substantially (e.g., GT-ERROR judged as 0.6% by GPT-4 vs 27.6% by Gemini-3-Pro), and there are no controlled experiments isolating LLM capacity from visual encoder/pretraining differences.

The SFT reasoning traces are generated by a proprietary VLM while conditioning on the ground-truth bounding box. This creates a serious leakage/ration-alization concern: the model is trained to imitate reasoning derived from the answer, and the paper never validates that the reasoning is faithful or causally necessary at inference time. Amodal reasoning data similarly appears to use modal/amodal boxes and direction guidance derived from ground truth.

The paper repeatedly claims 91.4 "IoU" when the reported metric is actually accuracy (IoU > 0.5). This misstatement appears in the abstract and conclusion and materially overstates the result. There are also table typos (e.g., "+0.07") and inconsistent improvement annotations.

The methodological novelty is limited. The approach is essentially SFT on proprietary reasoning traces followed by GRPO-style RL, which is standard. There is no comparison to simpler baselines such as direct distillation from a larger teacher model, token pruning/quantization, or efficient grounding-specific models.

The proprietary-model baselines are suspiciously weak (e.g., GPT-5 at 40.1 average accuracy on RefCOCO and 24.7 on amodal grounding), suggesting prompt/format mismatch rather than genuine model capability. Fair comparison across proprietary and open models is not established, and the 235B baselines are self-measured rather than taken from official reports.

The reasoning ablation is inconsistent and undermines the central claim. For Qwen3-VL-2B/4B, the no-reasoning variant already yields large gains; for InternVL-3-8B, the no-reasoning variant is worse than the base model. This suggests the gains may come from SFT/RL data curation rather than reasoning itself, yet the paper concludes that reasoning is essential.

The newly introduced amodal grounding benchmark is generated by a proprietary VLM with automatic filtering (about 50% removed) and no human verification of prompt quality or uniqueness. The benchmark may inherit stylistic biases from the generator and is not clearly released for reproducibility.

Reproducibility is limited because the main training data depends on proprietary VLM outputs, dataset/model release links are absent, and the proprietary model versions may not be stable. The substantial training cost of generating 575k reasoning traces and RL training is not reported.

The efficiency analysis is incomplete: it reports only average inference latency on a 10% subset and does not provide token counts, throughput, memory, energy, or latency distributions. Training cost and data-generation cost are ignored, yet the paper claims deployment-friendly efficiency.
The paper lacks a limitations discussion and does not address data licensing, potential biases in generated prompts, or societal impacts of using proprietary models for grounding data curation.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practical problem: efficient visual grounding for deployment-constrained settings, with a clear motivation that small VLMs lag behind larger ones and that reasoning/test-time compute can close the gap.

The empirical study is broad: the method is applied across InternVL-3 and Qwen3-VL families, multiple model sizes, vanilla grounding, and a newly introduced amodal grounding setting. The results consistently show gains over strong baselines.

The SFT+RL pipeline is well motivated and reasonably detailed. The use of reasoning traces, GRPO, and learnability-based RL data curation is coherent, and ablations support the importance of both SFT and RL, as well as the reasoning process.

The headline results are compelling: EGM-Qwen3-VL-8B achieves 91.4 average IoU on RefCOCO, surpassing Qwen3-VL-235B (90.5) while being 5.9x faster, and amodal grounding improves by large margins across model sizes.

The paper includes useful qualitative examples, efficiency comparisons, hard-sample analysis, and appendices with prompts and hyperparameters, which improves transparency relative to many comparable papers.
weaknesses: The causal claim that the small-vs-large VLM gap is mainly due to language understanding rather than visual encoding is not rigorously established. The failure analysis relies on proprietary models’ subjective categorization, with large variance across judges (e.g., COMPLEX-PROMPT 46.8–62.8%, GT-ERROR 0.6–27.6%), and does not fully rule out visual or data-side factors.

The method depends heavily on an unnamed proprietary VLM to generate SFT reasoning traces and amodal prompts. This limits reproducibility and raises questions about teacher quality, especially since the proprietary models shown are weaker than EGM on RefCOCO grounding.

For amodal grounding, both training prompts and evaluation prompts are generated by the same pipeline, which may introduce distribution bias and make the benchmark less independent. The paper also evaluates amodal performance only on COCO-Amodal-derived prompts, not on TAO-Amodal or human-verified annotations.

Efficiency claims focus on latency versus very large models, but a non-reasoning small model may be faster than EGM. The paper does not fully analyze output token length, latency breakdown, or whether the “many mid-quality tokens” argument is formally quantified beyond selected examples.

Some experiment details are unclear or inconsistent: table formatting/typos obscure the exact improvements, the RL reference model is InternVL-3.5-241B even for Qwen-family training, and code/data/model links appear absent in the manuscript. Full reproducibility is therefore uncertain.

The amodal grounding setting is interesting but the paper does not compare against specialized amodal segmentation/completion methods, so it is difficult to judge how much of the gain is due to the proposed reasoning framework versus the generated prompt/benchmark construction.
